accepted.label: b
accepted.text: A1: You may see versions like $4y\,\mathrm{d}y-6x\,\mathrm{d}y-6y\,\mathrm{d}x=14\mathrm{e}^{2x-1}\,\mathrm{d}x$ or $4yy'-6xy'-6y=14\mathrm{e}^{2x-1}$ which is acceptable. If they write $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=4y\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}-6x\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}-6y-14\mathrm{e}^{2x-1}=0$ this will be A0 unless the $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$ on the left subsequently disappears and is ignored.

Examples of acceptable reasons and acceptable conclusions are; E.g. I $\frac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{d}t}=-\frac{k}{4\pi r^2}=-\frac{c}{r^2}$, hence proven (Note that $c$ cannot be $k$) E.g. II $\frac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{d}t}=\frac{k}{4\pi r^2}$, as $\frac{k}{4\pi}$ is a constant $\frac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{d}t}\propto\frac{1}{r^2}$ Eg. III $\frac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{d}t}=-\frac{k}{4\pi r^2}$ as $k$ and $\pi$ are constants, it is true E.g. IV $\frac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{d}t}=-\frac{k}{4\pi r^2}=-\frac{k}{4\pi}\times\frac{1}{r^2}$ or $\left(-\frac{k}{4\pi}\right)\times\frac{1}{r^2}$ ✓
dM1: You may need to check calculations if the substitution isn't shown. You may see this attempted via $\left[\frac{y^2}{2}\right]_4^y=\left[\frac{3}{2}\sec 2x\right]_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^x$
A score of 1,0,1,1,1,1 is possible for candidates who never have a d$x$ and/or a d$y$ when separating the variables, but do everything else correctly.

ALT: A1: Correct separation of variables AND use of $\int\frac{\sin 2x}{\cos^2 2x}\mathrm{d}x\equiv(\cos 2x)^n$ where $n=-1$ or $-3$. If the candidate sets $u=\cos 2x$ it is for integrating $\int\frac{\sin 2x}{\cos^2 2x}\mathrm{d}x$ to $u^n$ where $n=-1$ or $-3$. M1: Correct attempted integration of the $\int\frac{\sin 2x}{\cos^2 2x}\mathrm{d}x$ to reach $\mathrm{f}(y)=\frac{\alpha}{\cos 2x}\,(+c)$ o.e with or without the $c$

Also note that you may attempt using integration by parts. FYI $\int 3\sin 2x\sec^2 2x\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{3}{2}\sin 2x\tan 2x+\frac{3}{2}\cos 2x$ 1st A1: Correct separation of variables and $\int 3\sin 2x\sec^2 2x\,\mathrm{d}x=\pm\lambda\sin 2x\tan 2x+\kappa\cos 2x$ $\lambda,\kappa>0$ 2nd M1: $\int 3\sin 2x\sec^2 2x\,\mathrm{d}x=\lambda\sin 2x\tan 2x\pm\kappa\cos 2x$ $\lambda,\kappa>0$ 2nd A1: $\int 3\sin 2x\sec^2 2x\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{3}{2}\sin 2x\tan 2x+\frac{3}{2}\cos 2x$

accepted.label: a
accepted.text: Other more complicated methods do exist so look carefully at what is attempted. For example, candidates could find $\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}y}$ at $t=2$ by finding $\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\div\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}$ and use the value of $-\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}y}$ as the gradient of the normal.

accepted.label: b
accepted.text: Other more complicated methods do exist but are unlikely to lead to any success. If you see a solution that you feel deserves credit please send to review and alert your TL. For example, if they start with $t=\sqrt{1-y}$ and then write down $x=\frac{3+2\sqrt{1-y}}{1-\sqrt{1-y}}$ the first M mark will not be scored until they make $\sqrt{1-y}$ the subject (in terms of just $x$) which reverts to the original method

accepted.label: b
accepted.text: If you see other methods that you feel deserve credit, and you cannot apply the scheme, then please send to review.
There will be many alternative approaches so you will need to look at what they have done to see if there is any credit worthy work. If in doubt please use review.

Alternative using $R$-alpha method: B1 M1: As above. A1*: Alternatively Considers $x\in(90^\circ,180^\circ)\Rightarrow(x+45^\circ)\in(135^\circ,225^\circ)$ and deduces that $\left|\sin(x+45^\circ)\right|<\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$ which means that $\left|\sqrt2\sin(x+45^\circ)\right|<1$ so meaning that the given statement is true

Alternative that proceeds via an identity in $\cos 2x$ and $\sin 2x$: M1: Squares $\left|\frac{\cos 2x}{\cos x-\sin x}\right|\geqslant1$ and uses suitable identities leading to an inequality in $\sin 2x$ and $\cos 2x$ dM1: Then uses Pythagoras identity A1*: ... therefore you have a contradiction and the original statement is true

Alternative using logic for the last two marks: dM1 Attempts to explain the contradiction by referencing the domain $90^\circ<x<180^\circ$ and corresponding range of values of (say) $\sin x$, $\cos x$. Must involve the modulus in their explanation or have squared previously. Stating that "$0<\sin x<1$ and $-1<\cos x<0$ for $90^\circ<x<180^\circ$", followed by " so $\left|\sin x+\cos x\right|<1$" would be a minimal but acceptable argument for dM1. Then the A1* is given for a completely rigorous explanation (plus conclusion)
